content: "Instead of discarding winter garden prunings by burning or shredding them, consider transforming them into a functional and ecologically beneficial dead hedge. This rustic structure not only serves as an effective windbreak to protect more delicate plants but also creates valuable shelter for insects, birds, and small mammals—enhancing biodiversity in your garden. To construct it, drive two parallel rows of sturdy stakes or reclaimed fence posts into the ground, spaced about 50 centimetres apart. Begin filling the gap with larger, sturdier branches at the base for stability, then layer in smaller twigs, stems, and other woody cuttings as you go. Over time, the hedge will naturally compact and settle, gaining structural integrity and aesthetic charm. On the lighter side of seasonal cheer, if your Christmas haul was underwhelming, treat yourself to something truly special: pre-order *The Book of Seeds*, a visually stunning and scientifically rich volume by Paul Smith—former director of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Scheduled for release in February and priced at £30 (Ivy Press), this lavishly illustrated guide explores 600 extraordinary seed species, from bizarrely textured specimens—like one evoking Donald Trump’s hairstyle—to minuscule orchid seeds no bigger than a pinhead. And for gardeners craving colour in the coldest months, winter-flowering clematis offers joyous, fragrant blooms from December through February. Cultivars such as *Clematis cirrhosa* ‘Advent Bells’ and its Balearic variety feature creamy, maroon-splashed flowers, while ‘Jingle Bells’ offers pure white, vigorous growth up to 5 metres tall. Is there anything else I can help with?"
